title: Union secures £15k towards unpaid Manchester Pride performer fees

input.lead: The performers went unpaid after the charity previously running Manchester Pride went bust in 2025
input.summary: The performers went unpaid after the charity previously running Manchester Pride went bust in 2025
input.evidence_text: Union secures £15k towards unpaid Manchester Pride performer fees - BBC News Image caption, Performers' union Equity says its unpaid members were "the heart of Manchester Pride" By Angela Ferguson North West Published 3 September 2026 A trade union representing some of the performers left unpaid after the charity running Manchester Pride went into administration said it has managed to secure £15,000. Equity said the money came from contributions from businesses within the "social action pot" put forward by Manchester City Council. It comes amid an ongoing Charity Commission investigation into the organisation which previously ran the event. Equity member and LGBTQ+ theatre-maker and activist Nathaniel Hall said it was "encouraging" news and, while the money would not cover all the losses, "the gesture is really welcome". Hall said LGBTQ+ Equity members "can be proud they have a union that has their backs when times are tough". The charity previously behind Manchester Pride entered voluntary liquidation in October 2025 . In a statement issued on 12 August, the Charity Commission said they were continuing to liaise with liquidators regarding Manchester Pride and their regulatory compliance case into the charity was ongoing. Image source, Stuart Rhoades Image caption, People have gathered in Manchester for the annual pride event for more than 40 years after its humble beginnings in 1985 Equity said it was contacting more than 50 performers who came forward to say they were owed £70,000. It said it would be distributing a percentage of unpaid fees to each artist, equating to about 20% of what they were owed. They said the funding, coupled with a £12,500 crowdfund sum organised by Nathaniel Hall brought the total raised to £27,500, almost 40% of the money owed. Equity North

title: Production at Kellogg's Trafford Park factory comes to an end

input.summary: The factory was built in 1938 and once produced a million boxes of cereal a day
input.evidence_text: Production at Kellogg's Trafford Park factory comes to an end - BBC News Image source, Peter McDermott Image caption, Production is moving to a Kellogg's site in Wrexham in north Wales By Richard Stead , Reporting from in Trafford Park and Angela Ferguson , North West Published 3 September 2026 Production at the Kellogg's factory in Greater Manchester has come to an end after almost 90 years, with the loss of about 360 jobs. The site in Trafford Park was one of the largest cereal factories in Europe when built in 1938 but production is being transferred to the company's site in Wrexham, north Wales. A spokesperson for owners Kellanova said the site has been a crucial part of its success for decades, adding: "We thank everyone who has worked there, as well as the suppliers, partners and local community who have worked alongside us." Mick Murray from retail union Usdaw said it was "a sad time" after working to "try to secure the best possible outcome for our members". In 2024 Kellanova announced that production of breakfast cereals would move to Wrexham, saying the investment required to maintain the factory was not viable. It came after the end of three-month talks with union and employee representatives . Marking the last week of production on site, a company spokesperson said: "A significant milestone was reached this week, as operations across production and packing came to an end." They said their priority through the transition has been to "support colleagues and the wider community through this period of change". input.summary: Allie Pottinger painted a mural for a hospital maternity unit's bereavement room

Regarded as the world’s most influential performance artist, Abramović’s transformative work has reached millions of people – from opening the Pyramid Stage at Glastonbury Festival t A four-hour ritual where ancient myth meets performance art, Balkan Erotic Epic explores the eroticism, spirituality and traditions of Abramović’s homeland through 13 visceral scenes Brought to life by a cast of over 70 performers, dancers, musicians and singers, the experience unfolds across Aviva Studios. Audiences are free to choose their own path – with pop-up encounters punctuating the action, bringing bodies together in dance, song and ritual Watch Fertility Rite , a fevered ritual where bodies writhe against the ground in a desperate call for fertility. Witness Massaging the Breast where women gesticulate over graves to awaken the earth. In Scaring the Gods , women bare themselves to the sky to banish storms. Listen Unafraid to push the boundaries of eroticism and performance art, Balkan Erotic Epic asks its audience a timeless question: What are our bodies truly for?
